subject: Computer Science
summary: Covers mobile computing and its limitations, cellular generations and GSM architecture, wireless LAN/Bluetooth/MANET and mobility, cloud computing (characteristics, IaaS/PaaS/SaaS, deployment, virtualisation), AI and machine learning basics, IoT, and other emerging technologies such as big data, blockchain, AR/VR and quantum computing. DSSSB asks full forms (GSM, GPRS), generation and speed ordering, cloud features, ML types and IoT challenges.

sections.heading: Mobile computing: concepts, limitations and mobile OS
sections.body:
**Mobile computing** lets users access data and services through portable devices while moving, using wireless communication. Its three parts are **mobile communication** (networks, protocols), **mobile hardware** (phones, tablets, wearables, sensors) and **mobile software** (mobile OS and apps).

**Characteristics**: device mobility, wireless connectivity, portability, location awareness, context awareness.
**Limitations**: limited **battery / power consumption**, limited **range and bandwidth**, **transmission interference** (weather, terrain, buildings), **security** risks of wireless links, small screens and keypads (**human interface** with the device), and possible health concerns.

**Mobile operating systems**: Android (Linux kernel based, Google), iOS (Apple), Symbian, Windows Mobile / Windows Phone, Palm OS, BlackBerry OS, KaiOS. ("MANET" is a network type, not an OS.)

**Mobile agents** are programs that migrate from host to host carrying their code and state, doing work locally and reducing network traffic; they are also called **transportable agents** and may follow a predefined path or an undefined (dynamic) path. **WAP** (Wireless Application Protocol) with **WML** was an early way to deliver web content to phones.

sections.heading: Cellular networks and generations
sections.body:
A **cellular network** divides an area into **cells**, each served by a base station. **Frequency reuse** lets distant cells use the same frequencies; a call moving between cells is passed on by **handoff (handover)** - hard (break before make) or soft (make before break, used in CDMA). Multiple access methods: **FDMA** (frequency division), **TDMA** (time slots), **CDMA** (unique codes, spread spectrum), **OFDMA** (orthogonal sub-carriers, used in 4G/5G).

Data speed increases in the order **GSM (circuit data) < GPRS < EDGE < UMTS/3G < HSPA < LTE (4G) < 5G**.

rows: very high speed, very low latency, massive IoT

sections.heading: GSM architecture and full forms
sections.body:
**GSM** = Global System for Mobile communication, a 2G digital standard using **TDMA** over FDMA carriers. Its architecture has these subsystems:
- **Mobile Station (MS)** = mobile equipment (identified by **IMEI**) + **SIM** (Subscriber Identity Module, holds the IMSI and keys).
- **Base Station Subsystem (BSS)**, the **radio subsystem**: **BTS** (Base Transceiver Station - radio with the phone) and **BSC** (Base Station Controller - manages several BTSs, handoffs, radio resources).
- **Network and Switching Subsystem (NSS)**: **MSC** (Mobile Switching Centre - call switching), **HLR** (Home Location Register - permanent subscriber database), **VLR** (Visitor Location Register - temporary data of subscribers currently in the area), **AuC** (Authentication Centre), **EIR** (Equipment Identity Register - valid/stolen handsets).
- **Operation Support Subsystem (OSS)** - network monitoring and maintenance (OMC).

Full forms: **GPRS** - General Packet Radio Service; **EDGE** - Enhanced Data rates for GSM Evolution; **UMTS** - Universal Mobile Telecommunications System; **LTE** - Long Term Evolution; **CDMA** - Code Division Multiple Access; **IMEI** - International Mobile Equipment Identity.

sections.heading: Wireless LANs, Bluetooth, MANET and mobility
sections.body:
- **Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11)** - wireless LAN; **infrastructure mode** (through an access point) or **ad hoc mode**. The **SSID** (Service Set Identifier) is a human-readable network name of **at most 32 bytes**, shared by all devices of a wireless network. Security: WPA2/WPA3 (WEP is insecure).
- **Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15.1)** - short-range 2.4 GHz personal area network; a **piconet** has one master and up to 7 active slaves; linked piconets form a **scatternet**.
- **Zigbee (IEEE 802.15.4)** - low power, low data rate mesh networking for sensors and IoT. **WiMAX (IEEE 802.16)** - wireless metropolitan networks. **NFC** - a few centimetres, contactless payments. **RFID** - tags read by radio.
- **Mobile IP** keeps a fixed home address while moving: **home agent**, **foreign agent**, **care-of address** and tunnelling.
- **MANET** (Mobile Ad hoc Network) - self-configuring, infrastructure-less network of mobile nodes that act as routers; topology changes constantly. Routing: reactive/on-demand (**AODV, DSR**), proactive/table-driven (**DSDV, OLSR**), hybrid (ZRP). Attacks: **black hole** (attracts and drops packets), **wormhole** (two colluding nodes tunnel packets to distort routes), **Byzantine** (compromised nodes inject false routing information, creating routing loops or non-optimal paths), sinkhole, Sybil.

**Types of mobility**: **macro-mobility** - movement across a global network (between domains); **micro-mobility** - movement within a local/regional network (between cells or subnets of one domain); **ad hoc mobility** - movement within a MANET, constantly changing its topology.

sections.heading: Cloud computing: characteristics, service and deployment models
sections.body:
**Cloud computing** (NIST) is a model for on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources (servers, storage, applications) that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort.

**Five essential characteristics**: **on-demand self-service**, **broad network access**, **resource pooling** (multi-tenancy), **rapid elasticity** (scalability) and **measured service** (pay-per-use).

**Service models**:
- **IaaS** (Infrastructure as a Service) - virtual machines, storage, networks; the user manages OS and apps (e.g. Amazon EC2, Google Compute Engine).
- **PaaS** (Platform as a Service) - runtime, middleware and tools to build and deploy apps (e.g. Google App Engine, Heroku).
- **SaaS** (Software as a Service) - complete applications through a browser (e.g. web mail, online office suites, CRM).
- Others: FaaS / serverless, DaaS (Desktop), STaaS (Storage).

**Deployment models**: **public** (shared by the general public, provider-owned), **private** (one organisation), **community** (several organisations with common concerns), **hybrid** (combination).

**Advantages**: no upfront capital cost, scalability, anywhere access, automatic updates, disaster recovery. **Concerns**: security and privacy, dependence on Internet connectivity, vendor lock-in, compliance and data location.

diagram.title: Who manages what
diagram.ascii:
Layer          On-premise   IaaS       PaaS       SaaS
 Application    you          you        you        provider

 Servers/Net    you          provider   provider   provider

sections.heading: Virtualisation, edge and fog computing
sections.body:
**Virtualisation** creates virtual versions of hardware so one physical machine runs several isolated **virtual machines (VMs)**; it is the foundation of cloud computing. The **hypervisor** (Virtual Machine Monitor) allocates resources:
- **Type 1 (bare-metal)** - runs directly on hardware: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Xen, KVM.
- **Type 2 (hosted)** - runs on a host OS: Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation.

**Containers** (e.g. Docker, orchestrated by Kubernetes) share the host OS kernel, so they are lighter and start faster than VMs. **SLA** (Service Level Agreement) defines the provider's guaranteed availability and performance.

**Edge computing** processes data near its source (on devices or local gateways) to reduce latency and bandwidth; **fog computing** adds an intermediate layer of nodes between edge devices and the cloud. Both suit IoT and real-time applications.

sections.heading: Artificial intelligence: foundations
sections.body:
**Artificial Intelligence (AI)** is the science of making machines perform tasks that need human intelligence - reasoning, learning, perception, language understanding and problem solving. The term was coined by **John McCarthy** (1956, Dartmouth conference). The **Turing Test** (Alan Turing, 1950) judges whether a machine's conversation is indistinguishable from a human's.

- **Narrow (weak) AI** - one specific task (voice assistants, recommendation); **General (strong) AI** - human-level ability across tasks (not yet achieved); **super AI** - hypothetical.
- **Intelligent agent** - perceives its environment through sensors and acts through actuators; described by **PEAS** (Performance, Environment, Actuators, Sensors).
- **Search**: uninformed (BFS, DFS) and informed/heuristic (best-first, **A*** with f(n) = g(n) + h(n)); game playing with minimax and alpha-beta pruning.
- **Knowledge representation**: propositional and predicate logic, semantic networks, frames, production rules. AI languages: **LISP**, **Prolog**, Python.
- Branches: machine learning, **NLP** (natural language processing), computer vision, robotics, expert systems, speech recognition.
- Concerns: **bias**, lack of explainability (**black-box** models), privacy, deepfakes, job displacement.

sections.heading: Machine learning and deep learning
sections.body:
**Machine learning (ML)** lets systems learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed.
- **Supervised learning** - labelled data. **Classification** (discrete labels: spam/not spam) and **regression** (continuous values: price). Algorithms: linear and logistic regression, decision trees, random forest, k-nearest neighbours, naive Bayes, support vector machines.
- **Unsupervised learning** - unlabelled data: **clustering** (k-means), association rules, dimensionality reduction (PCA).
- **Reinforcement learning** - an agent learns by trial and error from **rewards and penalties** (games, robotics).
- **Semi-supervised** learning uses a few labels plus much unlabelled data.

**Model evaluation**: split into training and test sets; **overfitting** = fits training data but fails on new data; **underfitting** = too simple. Confusion-matrix metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1.

**Neural networks**: layers of artificial neurons computing a weighted sum plus bias passed through an **activation function** (step, sigmoid, ReLU); trained by **backpropagation** with gradient descent. **Deep learning** uses many hidden layers: **CNNs** for images, **RNN/LSTM** for sequences, **transformers** for language. **Generative AI** (large language models, GANs) creates new text, images or audio.

**Data handling in Python (pandas)**: a **Series** is a one-dimensional labelled array of any data type; a **DataFrame** is a two-dimensional labelled table whose columns may have different types.

code.source:
actual    = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0]
predicted = [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0]

tp = sum(a == 1 and p == 1 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
tn = sum(a == 0 and p == 0 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
fp = sum(a == 0 and p == 1 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
fn = sum(a == 1 and p == 0 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))

accuracy  = (tp + tn) / len(actual)
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall    = tp / (tp + fn)
f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
print("TP TN FP FN:", tp, tn, fp, fn)
print(f"accuracy={accuracy:.2f} precision={precision:.2f} recall={recall:.2f} f1={f1:.2f}")

sections.heading: Internet of Things (IoT)
sections.body:
**IoT** is a network of physical objects ("things") embedded with **sensors, actuators, software and connectivity** that collect and exchange data and can be controlled remotely.

**Components**: sensors/actuators → connectivity (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth Low Energy, Zigbee, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, cellular) → **gateway** → cloud/edge processing and analytics → user application.
**Architecture**: 3-layer - **perception** (sensing), **network** (transmission), **application** (services); the 5-layer version adds processing (middleware) and business layers.
**Protocols**: **MQTT** (lightweight publish-subscribe via a broker over TCP), **CoAP** (RESTful, over UDP, for constrained devices), **6LoWPAN** (IPv6 over low-power wireless), RFID and NFC. **IPv6** provides enough addresses for billions of devices.
**Applications**: smart homes, smart cities, wearables and remote health monitoring, precision agriculture, industrial IoT (**Industry 4.0**), smart grids, vehicle tracking.
**Challenges of IoT adoption**: **security** (weak default passwords, unpatched devices, botnets), privacy, interoperability and standards, power and battery life, scalability, data management.

sections.heading: Other emerging technologies
sections.body:
- **Big data** - datasets too large or fast for traditional tools; the **5 Vs**: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value. Tools: **Hadoop** (HDFS storage + MapReduce processing), Apache Spark, NoSQL databases.
- **Blockchain** - a decentralised, distributed **ledger** of blocks, each holding transactions and the **hash of the previous block**, which makes the chain tamper-evident (immutable). Consensus by **Proof of Work** or **Proof of Stake**; **smart contracts** are self-executing code on the chain; cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin are one application.
- **AR** (Augmented Reality) overlays digital content on the real world; **VR** (Virtual Reality) is fully immersive and computer-generated; **MR** mixes both.
- **3D printing** (additive manufacturing) builds objects layer by layer from a digital model.
- **Quantum computing** uses **qubits**, which exploit **superposition** and **entanglement**.
- **Robotics** and **RPA** (Robotic Process Automation - software bots for repetitive office tasks); drones; **digital twins** (virtual replicas of physical systems).
- **Geolocation** services let users share their location with websites and apps they trust.

workedExamples.problem: Practice: A cellular system has 840 duplex channels and uses a 7-cell cluster (i = 2, j = 1). Find the channels per cell and the co-channel reuse distance if the cell radius is 2 km.
Practice: A classifier's results on 10 test cases give TP = 4, TN = 3, FP = 2, FN = 1 (as in the Python program). Compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1.
Practice: Run one round of k-means (k = 2) on the 1-D data 2, 4, 6, 15, 18, 22, 25 with initial centroids 3 and 20.
workedExamples.solution:
Assign each point to the nearer centroid:
- 2, 4, 6 → centroid 3 (distances 1, 1, 3 versus 18, 16, 14).
- 15 → centroid 20 (distance 5 versus 12); 18, 22, 25 → centroid 20.
New centroids: (2 + 4 + 6) ÷ 3 = **4**; (15 + 18 + 22 + 25) ÷ 4 = 80 ÷ 4 = **20**.
Re-assigning with 4 and 20 gives the same clusters (15 is 11 from 4 and 5 from 20), so the algorithm has converged: clusters {2, 4, 6} and {15, 18, 22, 25}.

workedExamples.problem: Practice: A neuron has inputs x = (1, 0, 1), weights w = (0.5, −0.4, 0.3), bias b = −0.6 and a step activation (output 1 if net ≥ 0, else 0). Find the output. What if the bias were −0.9?

Identify the cloud service model: (a) a startup rents virtual servers and installs its own OS and database; (b) developers upload code and the provider handles runtime, scaling and OS; (c) a school uses browser-based e-mail and documents; (d) which deployment model is a government department's own data centre shared with no one else?
workedExamples.solution:
(a) **IaaS** - user manages OS and above.
(b) **PaaS** - provider manages the platform; user manages only the application and data.
(c) **SaaS** - complete application delivered over the web.
(d) **Private cloud**.

pitfalls: CDMA was used in 2G (IS-95) as well as in 3G (WCDMA, CDMA2000); in exam keys 'CDMA' alone usually means 2G.
GPRS = General Packet Radio Service (not 'Radiation' or 'Package').
HLR stores permanent subscriber data; VLR stores temporary data of visiting subscribers.
Device mobility and wireless connectivity are characteristics of mobile computing, not limitations.
SSID can be at most 32 bytes, not 2000 bytes.
Wormhole attack tunnels packets between colluding nodes; a Byzantine attack injects false routing information to create loops.
Pay-per-use = measured service; scalability = rapid elasticity; both are essential cloud characteristics.
Type 1 hypervisor runs on bare metal; Type 2 runs on a host OS.
Classification predicts categories; regression predicts continuous values; clustering is unsupervised.
Security is the main challenge of IoT adoption; deepfakes and black-box models are AI-ethics issues.
A pandas Series is 1-D; a DataFrame is 2-D with columns of possibly different types.
